definition: Implacable means impossible to appease or calm.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word implacable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know implacable should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Ten years of birthday cards changed nothing; Aunt Marisol stayed implacable about the borrowed, never-returned pearls.
Someone displeased is unhappy about it today and over it by the weekend; implacable anger is the opposite pole — years of apologies leave it exactly where it began.
The unforgiving never pardon the offense; the implacable go further — no apology, gift, or offering will even lower the temperature.

Unappeasable makes the same claim in transparent parts — no offering will ever satisfy — and it fastens onto appetites and demands as readily as anger: an unappeasable hunger, an unappeasable crowd. Implacable is the darker, narrower word for a person whose settled hostility no apology or gift will soften.

Relentless is about pressure that never lets up — the relentless questioning, the relentless pace — force applied and kept on. Implacable faces the other direction: it measures what comes in, reporting that no apology, plea, or peace offering will ever soften the anger. One never stops pushing; the other can never be soothed.

When the Hendersons' oak dropped a limb through his greenhouse, Mr.
Voss refused the apology, refused the repair crew, and refused the replacement panes bought and paid for in advance.
Fruit baskets came back unopened; a driveway-shoveling campaign one snowy winter earned a single nod and no thaw.
Twenty years on, he still turns his back at the mailbox.
Angry passes; even furious burns itself out.
Implacable is a different claim: the anger has no price.
The word doesn't measure heat — it reports that every instrument of soothing has been tried on this person and has failed, and that the next attempt will fail too.
Implacable says every instrument of soothing has failed or will: implacable enemies, implacable critics, an implacable sense of grievance.
Its unit-mate irascible measures how fast anger lights; implacable measures whether it can ever be put out.
The irascible flare and cool; the implacable never cool at all.

In the 1870s two of America's leading fossil hunters, once friendly enough to name species after each other, fell into a feud that would consume both careers.
The younger man tried repeatedly to repair it.
He wrote letters praising his rival's monographs, offered to share a promising quarry in Wyoming, and once proposed a joint expedition, with the elder man to lead.
The elder scientist proved implacable: he returned the letters, refused the quarry, and told a reporter he would sooner burn his notes than co-sign a paper.
Colleagues marveled that the offers themselves seemed to feed the anger, each olive branch catalogued as a fresh insult.
When the younger man died first, editors expected a softening obituary.
The one that arrived instead settled, for historians, any doubt about how deep the grudge ran.
